messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: sub sampling the posterior [rstan]
parts:
Hi!

I find myself regularly to sub-sample my posterior and wonder if this is either already implemented in rstan or should be added? The thing is, I like to run multiple chains and keep a decent amount of samples from those chains to ensure sampling diagnostics work well. However, working with the sample is often sufficient with a fraction of what I sampled. Therefore, I tend to only take a few 100 draws instead of 1k or so. The sub-sampling is easy to do, but this could be a useful feature for others maybe.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: sub sampling the posterior [rstan]
parts:
I thought thinning is applied as the samples are being generated. So thinning throws away immediately draws and hence the diagnostics are not as good nor can I look at traceplots that detailed. Moreover, I often like to do analyses quick and dirty and then maybe do it one more time the "proper" way with the full sample. I think this is not yet available in Stan, but instead I have to subset the sample myself always which is just a little inconvenient.

S

parts:
I'm still not sure what you're proposing. Is it something
like the following?

fit <- stan(...);
fit.ss <- thin(fit, N);

that'll take N random draws from the fit and return another
fit object?

I still have no idea why you'd want to do this. Do you have
code that's slow to run over 4000 draws that is fast over 400
draws? Reducing to 400 throws away information, so we almost always
just use all the draws we save.

- Bob

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sub sampling the posterior [rstan]
parts:
We (with Juho and Markus) have also an example were we obtain 4000 draws, check the diagnostics, and then would like to further computation with as few draws as possible. It's better to choose the smaller number of draws determinisitically and not randomly. For example, to pick 40 draws, simple deterministic approach is to pick every 100th draw from each chain (not from the permuted draws!). In our case we might be willing to use even more computationally intensive deterministic method (such as support points https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01811) which would give lower variance for the further estimates than the simple approach mentioned above. An example of slow computation is projection predictive model reduction for some models. For us, rstan support for thinning is low priority as the basic thinning is so easy to do anyway (and the support point method would require additional testing).

Aki
